title: Eco-Friendly Free-Standing Conductive PEDOT-based Nonwovens for Wearable and Flexible Touch Sensors
abstract: Abstract This work focuses on the development of eco-friendly, free-standing conductive nonwovens electrospun from poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) and polyethylene oxide (PEO) for applications in flexible and wearable electronics. The study advances the understanding of PEDOT-based nanofiber mats by employing thermal treatment to enhance their conductivity, followed by extensive electrical, mechanical, and electrochemical characterization. A novel aspect of this research is the environmental evaluation of these materials through ecotoxicological assays. Tests conducted on freshwater and marine organisms, including bacteria, algae, and crustaceans, simulate the potential impact of these nonwoven materials on aquatic ecosystems and address both freshwater compatibility and the unexplored marine toxicity. The findings indicate that the PEDOT-based nonwovens exhibit improved conductivity and mechanical strength upon thermal treatment, while maintaining environmental compatibility. The study also demonstrates the practical application of these materials in a sensorized prototype glove suitable for rehabilitation, highlighting their potential for use in advanced wearable technologies. This multidisciplinary approach bridges material innovation and environmental responsibility by examining the sustainable use of conductive polymers in wearable devices. Overall, the findings highlight the intersection of advances in electrospun nanomaterials and environmental sustainability, contributing to advancements in wearable technologies while promoting eco-responsible material usage. sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The production of nanofibers has emerged as a crucial research area due to their unique properties and extensive applications across biomedicine, energy, textiles, and environmental science. Among the various methods for producing nanofibers, electrospinning has gained significant attention. This method is versatile, scalable, and capable of producing nanofibers with tailored properties, which makes it highly appealing for both scientific research and industrial applications [ 1 ,  2 – 3 ]. Electrospinning uses a high-voltage electric field to draw a thin jet of polymer solution from a hollow needle; as the jet stretches and the solvent evaporates, it forms continuous nanofibers. The nanofibers produced by this method typically exhibit diameters ranging from a few hundred nanometers to several micrometers, with exceptional uniformity and purity. One of the key advantages of electrospun nanofibers is their high surface-to-volume ratio, which enhances their interaction with the environment. This makes them ideal for various applications, including filtration, drug delivery, tissue engineering, and sensing technologies. Moreover, electrospinning enables significant tunability: by adjusting parameters such as polymer concentration, solvent type, applied voltage, and collection distance, researchers can tailor the properties of the nanofibers to meet specific application needs. In addition to tunability, electrospinning offers scalability and cost-effectiveness, making it suitable for large-scale production. The simplicity of the process and its ability to consistently produce uniform and pure nanofibers further enhance its industrial potential.

Conductive polymers have been an area of growing interest due to their unique combination of electrical conductivity, mechanical flexibility, and ease of processing. This opens new possibilities for developing advanced electronic devices and energy storage systems. Several conductive polymers, such as polyaniline (PANI), polypyrrole (PPy), and polythiophenes, have been extensively studied. However, among these, poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT) has shown great promise due to its high conductivity, environmental stability, and ease of synthesis [ 4 ,  5 ]. PEDOT belongs to the polythiophene family and is characterized by its π-conjugated structure, which imparts high electrical conductivity to the material. The ethylenedioxy functional groups, thanks to their polarity and hydrophilicity, enhance PEDOT’s solubility and processability, making it easy to fabricate into thin films, coatings, and composites. In addition, PEDOT exhibits remarkable environmental stability, particularly under ambient conditions, wherein many other conductive polymers tend to degrade [ 6 ,  7 – 8 ]. This stability makes PEDOT suitable for applications requiring long-term durability, such as organic electronics and biosensors.

Additionally, PEDOT's electrical and optical properties are tunable through chemical doping, allowing its conductivity and transparency to be adjusted for specific applications, including transparent electrodes and optoelectronics. One of the most commercially available forms of PEDOT is its dispersion in water, stabilized by polystyrene sulfonate (PSS). In addition to its high surface area-to-volume ratio, electrospinning PEDOT enables precise control over the diameter and alignment of nanofibers, which in turn influence their mechanical strength and conductivity. Electrospun PEDOT nanofibers have gained importance in bioelectronics, as they allow for the creation of bioactive interfaces with enhanced conductivity, mechanical properties, and biocompatibility [ 9 ,  10 ]. These interfaces are crucial for developing advanced biomedical devices such as biosensors, neural implants, and drug delivery systems. The evolution of PEDOT nanofibers produced through electrospinning has led to significant improvements in their conductivity and mechanical properties. Early approaches involved fabricating PEDOT nanofibers by electrospinning insulating polymers, followed by vapor-phase polymerization of PEDOT. More recent advancements include the use of oxidative polymerization and blending PEDOT with other polymers, such as polyethylene oxide (PEO), for solution-based electrospinning, which further enhances the conductivity, flexibility, and structural stability of the nanofibers [ 11 ,  12 ]. These innovations have positioned PEDOT nanofibers as promising materials for flexible electronics, sensors, and biomedical devices, with the potential to drive further advancements in these fields [ 13 ,  14 ,  15 ,  16 ,  17 – 18 ]. While PEDOT and PEDOT-based materials have attracted significant interest as organic conductors, understanding their mechanical properties is paramount to enable their reliable use in practical applications, including emerging fields such as wearable and implantable electronic devices for healthcare [ 19 ].

Due to its water solubility and environmental stability, PEDOT could leach into environments and potentially impact aquatic ecosystems. For instance, recent studies have reported that PEDOT polystyrene sulfonate (PSS) negatively impacts freshwater ecosystems by inhibiting algal growth and chlorophyll production and impairing fish behavior and development [ 20 ]. Conversely, the biocompatibility of the PEDOT:PSS and PEO composite nanofibers was demonstrated in the aquatic system towards microalgae and cyanobacteria [ 21 ]. Besides these limited studies on the toxicity of nonwoven materials in freshwater, no data is currently available on the potential environmental risk to the marine ecosystem. Increasing knowledge on the toxicity and eco-compatibility of these materials in both freshwater and seawater aquatic environments is of great interest to ensure responsible and sustainable material use, as materials often end up in natural aquatic systems [ 20 ].

This study developed electrospun PEDOT nonwovens for flexible, wearable electronics, including PEDOT mats with enhanced conductivity via thermal treatment (PEDOT-TT). Their electrical, mechanical, and electrochemical properties were thoroughly assessed to determine suitability for advanced technological applications. Suitability was further demonstrated by the development of a basic sensorized glove prototype using the electrospun nanofiber mat as a sensor. Furthermore, the study uniquely investigates the environmental impact of fabricated nonwoven materials, evaluating their aquatic ecotoxicity to address sustainability concerns. Additionally, the environmental compatibility of fabricated PEDOT-based nonwovens has been studied in freshwater and seawater through ecotoxicological tests to address sustainability concerns. Although nonwoven materials’ toxicity assessment has been studied in freshwater ecosystems [ 20 ], the marine ecosystem has not yet been investigated. Therefore, we aimed at filling this current gap by assessing the safety and eco-compatibility of PEDOT-based nonwovens in the marine environment. Specifically, a battery of bioassays has been applied to both marine and freshwater organisms (bacteria, algae, and crustaceans) to assess the toxicity of non-woven materials in organisms at the first levels of the aquatic trophic chain. This multidisciplinary approach bridges material innovation with environmental responsibility, offering novel insights into the potential and implications of such materials in real-world applications.

sections.heading: Morphological Characterization
paragraphs: Successful nanofiber production was observed at relatively low concentrations of PEO and PEDOT (< 90 µmol·L −1  and < 20 µmol·L −1 , respectively), while higher concentrations led to process failure (Fig.  S1 ). The spinnability of the solutions is constrained at high PEO concentrations, as increased viscosity limits the process (as shown on the right side of the diagram). Additionally, high PEDOT concentrations (> 20 µmol·L −1 ) disrupt the electric field between the needle and collector due to the polymer's conductivity [ 22 ,  23 ]. The high-quality nanofibers obtained, characterized by uniformity over large areas and an average diameter of 210 ± 50 nm, are shown in Fig.  S1 b-d and Fig.  S2 . The rheological behavior of the solutions exhibits pseudoplasticity, with viscosity decreasing as shear rate increases (Fig.  S1 e). Using smaller needles at the same flow rate improves the spinning process by reducing the local viscosity This adjustment extends the spinnability region toward higher PEO concentrations, offering valuable insights for enhancing industrial-scale PEDOT nanofiber production and yield. The optimal combination of spinnability and performance was achieved with PEDOT PH1000 and PEO concentrations of 18 µmol·L −1  and 69 µmol·L −1 , respectively. This solution was used to produce nonwoven samples and subsequently to manufacture PEDOT-based sensors.

The thermal treatment of PEDOT nanofibers effectively induced cross-linking reactions between the polymeric chains of PSS and PEO, as reported in the literature [ 24 ,  73 ,  74 ]. This process resulted in a more structured nanofiber network, enhancing mechanical strength and water resistance. Specifically, the cross-linking chemically modifies the molecular structure of the polymer chains, rendering the reacted PEO insoluble in water. FT-IR spectra reported in Fig.  1 a show the characteristic absorption bands for PEDOT:PSS PH1000 water dispersion, PEO, and the electrospun nanofiber before and after thermal treatment. The FT-IR peaks for PEDOT:PSS correspond to vibrations of the sulfonate groups in PSS (centered at 1170 cm −1  and 1012 cm −1 ), and the stretching of the C–S–C bond in the thiophene ring at 961, 916, 838, and 674 cm −1  [ 25 ,  26 ]. PEO exhibits several bands in its fingerprint region, mainly associated with wagging, twisting, and rocking of CH 2  groups (respectively at 1365–1335 cm −1 , 1290–1230 cm −1 , and 970–830 cm −1 ) and stretching of C–O at 1099 cm −1  [ 27 ]. In the nonwoven samples, characteristic vibrations of both PEDOT:PSS and PEO can be observed, albeit with a reduced intensity, indicating the successful deposition of both constituents in the nanofibers. Furthermore, thermal treatment promotes changes in the relative intensities of specific bands: in Fig.  1 b it is possible to observe a significant reduction in the broad absorption band of –OH in the range 3500–3000 cm −1  when comparing samples before and after thermal treatment. In the fingerprint region, Fig.  1 c, the sulfonate band of PSS located at 1170 cm −1  decreases in intensity, while the C–O absorption at 1099 cm −1  notably increases after thermal treatment. While some band overlapping occurs due to the complexity of PEDOT:PSS, the overall trends are reproducible and align with published PSS/PEO crosslinking studies [ 24 ,  73 ,  74 ]. The reported FT-IR analysis supports the rationale that thermal treatment activates condensation between PEO hydroxyl groups and the sulfonic acid groups of PSS, forming sulfonate-ester (SO 2 –O–C) crosslinks. These interchain bridges increase polymer cohesion, reduce inter-fiber slippage and maximum strain, and decrease the number of free hydrophilic groups (–OH and –SO 3 − ), thereby enhancing both mechanical integrity and water resistance of the nanofiber network. The newly formed bonds between PEO and PSS contribute to a stronger nonwoven structure, enabling a more uniform stress distribution. The effects of thermal treatment on the morphology of nonwovens are illustrated in Fig.  2 a-f, which reveal the reduced thickness and visible waviness of a PEDOT nanofiber mat after thermal treatment, while Fig.  2 g,h present the macroscopic appearance of the samples. As reported in the literature, crosslinking does not affect the thermal properties of nonwovens (Fig.  2 i), as the high molecular weight PEO maintains its degree of crystallinity after the thermal treatment [ 24 ,  73 ]. Fig. 1 a  FT-IR spectra of PEDOT:PSS PH1000, PEO, as-spun and thermally treated nonwovens.  b  Reduction of the absorption band of the hydroxyl group in as-spun and thermally treated samples.  c  Main absorption bands in the fingerprint region from PEO (light grey) and PEDOT:PSS (dark grey) Fig. 2 SEM images of PEDOT-based nanofibers.  a  Top view.  b , c  Cross-sections of as-spun samples (Scale bar in Fig. b: 100 μm; Scale bar in Fig. c: 10 μm);  d  Top view and  e , f  Cross-sections after thermal treatment in vacuum (Scale bar in Fig. e: 50 μm; Scale bar in Fig. f: 10 μm). The average thickness is 29 μm for the untreated nonwoven and 5 μm for the thermally treated one.  g , h  Macroscopic optical photograph of as-spun and thermally treated samples, respectively.  i  DSC thermograms of samples

Chemical and co-solvent doping methods such as EG, DMSO, ionic liquids, or strong acid soaking typically yield conductivity enhancements in the range of 10 2 –10 3 x (e.g., 2000 × for EG [ 28 ], 670 × for DMSO [ 29 ], and up to 4000 × for nitric acid treatment [ 30 ]). Although thermal treatment produces a more modest conductivity enhancement compared with stronger doping strategies, it offers a simple, substrate-compatible, and reproducible method for tuning the electrical performance of PEDOT:PSS films.

The XPS survey spectra for the as-spun and thermally treated samples are presented in Fig.  3 a. The main elements present at the surface of the samples are C and O, as evidenced by the presence of the pronounced C 1s and O 1s photoemission peaks at approximately 286 eV and 533 eV, respectively. The corresponding KLL Auger transitions are also clearly visible at high binding energy. Minor features at 168 and 230 eV, assigned respectively to the S 2p and S 2s core levels, are also predominantly present in the as-spun sample. High-resolution core-level spectra (Fig.  3 b) provide a more detailed view into the chemical changes induced by the thermal treatment. In the S 2p, there is a substantial reduction in intensity, while in O 1 s and C 1 s, there is a decrease in the lower binding energy feature. Quantitative analysis indicates that the S content decreases from 2.3% to 0.4% (in atomic concentration). In the S 2p spectrum, the low binding energy doublet (S 2p 3/2  at 163.5 eV) is attributed to the thiophene of PEDOT. The feature at a larger binding energy is instead due to the PSS sulfonate group. Following the literature assignment, two different species can be identified: the doublet at 167.9 eV is associated with the deprotonated sulfonate (-SO 3 − ) species, while the component at 169.3 eV corresponds to the neutral form (-SO 3 H) [ 31 ,  32 – 33 ]. The relative PEDOT:PSS sulfur ratio is approximately 40:60 in the as-spun sample and 35:65 after thermal treatment; however, due to the lower S/N ratio in the thermally treated sample, this variation is not considered significant. Fig. 3 a  XPS spectra recorded for the as-spun (black) and thermally treated samples (red). The peaks present in the full range scans indicate the presence of C, O, and S.  b  Narrow scans of the O 1s, C 1s, and S 2p photoemission lines. The data for the S 2p line has been multiplied by a factor of 50

The overall loss of S intensity is explained by the formation of a thin PEO overlayer on the nanofiber surface rather than by the thermal degradation of the PEDOT:PSS polymers which is not expected at the temperatures used in the treatment. Consistently, no new chemical features appear in either the C 1 s or O 1 s spectra. Indeed, the components primarily associated with PEO [ 34 ,  35 ] (C–O–C, C–OH at 286.5 and 533 eV) remain essentially unchanged, while the components at lower binding energy, mostly linked to PSS (SO 3  at 531.4 eV) and PEDOT:PSS (C–S and C = C at 285 eV), decrease. Therefore, we do not identify any clear indication of cross-linking in XPS; this can be rationalized due to the extremely limited amount of cross-links compared to the number of C–O bonds in the high molecular weight PEO (600 kDa), considering also that the difference in binding energy for these types of bond is smaller than the resolution of XPS in these experimental conditions. XPS is a core-electron spectroscopic technique; therefore, it is less sensitive to the chemical environment than vibrational techniques like FT-IR or Raman. Since the XPS analysis depth is limited to only a few nanometers, the PEO overlayer must be thin. To confirm the presence of PEDOT:PSS beneath this layer, we performed depth-profiling measurement by sputtering with Ar +   ions, despite the known susceptibility of soft polymeric materials to ion-induced damage (see Figure  S3 ). The intensity of sulfur increases already after short sputtering time (between 30 and 120 s at 1 kV), supporting the presence of buried PEDOT:PSS. But the sputtering-induced damage prevents reliable quantitative or systematic analysis.

sections.heading: Electrochemical and Electromechanical Properties
paragraphs: The equipment for electrochemical characterization is shown in Fig.  S4 a. EIS spectra (Fig.  S4 b), represented in the Nyquist plots, show the presence of two processes; a semicircle in the high-frequency portion and a tail toward lower frequencies, indicating an increase in impedance as the signal frequency decreases. The first process can be attributed to the formation of a double layer at the sample-solution interface. In contrast, the second one can be attributed to the electrode’s blocking behavior, which can absorb a limited amount of ions. The spectra measured after CV preserved their shape, indicating high stability under the testing conditions, without introducing or removing processes. A change in the high-frequency process toward lower resistance values, highlighted an improvement of the sample/solution interaction by reducing the charge-transfer resistance. Such variation indicates that the material interaction is activated by applying the CV scan. Cyclic voltammetry is a key method for evaluating the reversibility of PEDOT:PSS charge–discharge behavior. During cycling, the nonwoven material may undergo physical changes caused by interactions between charge carriers and the conductive polymer. Fig.  S4 c demonstrates that the material maintains its mechanical stability and cyclic voltammetry profile across multiple scan speeds without degradation, emphasizing its potential for applications such as sensing. Cyclic voltammograms exhibited the expected capacitive behavior of the PEDOT-based samples [ 36 ,  37 ], with symmetrical oxidation/reduction peaks, indicating the reversibility of the processes occurring at the sample interface. By plotting the main peak current as a function of the potential scan rate (Fig.  S4 d), a linear trend emerges, indicating a surface-controlled process rather than one governed by diffusion. This behavior suggests that redox species are adsorbed on the electrode surface rather than diffusing freely in solution. With adsorbed redox species, the number of molecules available for electron transfer remains constant, independent of bulk diffusion. Consequently, peak current scales proportionally with scan rate, as faster rates enable more electron transfers per unit time. The observed linearity confirms that the rate-limiting factor is electron transfer or adsorption/desorption at the electrode surface. This aligns with the characteristics of nonwoven samples: the nanofibers' high surface-to-volume ratio facilitates interaction of conducting species at their surfaces, minimizing the role of diffusion in the overall process.

The electrical response of the tested materials throughout the entire frequency range exhibited negligible phase shifts, indicating predominantly resistive behavior. This characteristic is evident as plateaus in the Bode plots, where the impedance modulus (| Z |) is plotted as a function of frequency, as shown in Fig.  4 a-d. The impedance data obtained in this manner were plotted against the mechanical load for both samples. The thermally treated sample consistently exhibited lower resistance than the as-spun sample (see Fig.  4 e). Upon increasing the mechanical pressure, both samples exhibited an asymptotic reduction in resistance, though at different decay rates, resulting in a minimized resistance difference between the two samples at higher pressures. The variation in the linear fit slope, reported in Fig.  4 f, is associated with the hopping mechanism of electron transfer between chains, in accordance with the power law model for the material reported in the literature [ 38 ]. The variation of slope from -1.03 to -0.58, with a consequent increase in electrical conductivity in the thermally treated sample, can be related to the formation of cross-links during thermal treatment and to the variation of morphology and increase in the size of the nodes between nanofibers as shown in high-resolution SEM images (Fig.  2 d) induced by thermal treatment. Furthermore, the reduction in material thickness is correlated with the formation of novel inter-nanofiber connections. This occurs, for example, during thermal treatment or when the material is loaded in compression during use. Fig. 4 a , b  Electrical response as a function of applied pressure on the untreated nonwoven and  c , d  on the thermally treated sample. Arrows and insets indicate the area zoomed in for clarity.  e  Trends in the real part of the impedance with increasing applied pressure and  f  linear fitting of the log–log plot

A force-sensing resistor (FSR) is a sensor whose electrical resistance decreases in response to applied mechanical pressure, enabling it to detect force through changes in conductivity [ 39 ,  40 ]. In conductive polymer-based FSRs, this behaviour is often governed by a percolation mechanism, where pressure-induced changes in the material's internal structure increase the number and quality of conductive pathways [ 41 ]. Impedance measurements of the PEDOT-based nonwovens reveal predominantly resistive behaviour across the frequency range, with resistance decreasing asymptotically as mechanical load increases. This pressure-dependent electrical response, particularly the reduced resistance under compression and the enhanced conductivity in thermal-treated samples due to morphological changes, confirms the material's functionality as an FSR. In the data reported in Fig.  4 f, since the trends follow a power law, the sensitivity to compression of the nonwoven material is indicated by the exponent (i.e., the slope of the linear fit). It is worth noting that, while thermal treatment improves the electrical performance (i.e., conductivity) of the material, it decreases its sensitivity (−0.85 Ω·g −1 ·cm 2  for as-spun nonwoven versus −0.25 Ω·g −1 ·cm 2  for thermally treated samples). By adjusting the duration of the thermal treatment to control nanofiber node density, the trade-off between sensitivity and conductivity can be systematically tuned to meet the requirements of different applications.

sections.heading: Analytical and Geometrical Modeling of Transverse Resistance in Compressed Nanofiber Layers
paragraphs: This theoretical resistance is several orders of magnitude lower than the experimentally measured value of approximately 100 Ω at zero external pressure (see Fig.  4 e). This discrepancy suggests that the transverse resistance is not dominated by the intrinsic material properties, but rather, by contact resistances and structural discontinuities in the nanofiber network. Therefore, it is not possible to treat the material as an ideal bulk, but instead, the number of connecting nodes between nanofibers must be considered.

This calculated value of transverse resistance is in the same order of magnitude as the experimental one, indicating the consistency of our approach. We expect that, while increasing the pressure, the number of contacts increases too, thus causing an increase in the number of possible parallel paths and then a decrease of the transverse resistance, in accordance with data shown in Fig.  4 d. Furthermore, we note that the resistance is systematically lower for the thermally treated fibers, indicating a lower contact resistance due to the promotion of more efficient percolation paths.

To model the increase in inter-fiber connectivity under mechanical compression, we developed a geometric and statistical framework describing the behavior of nanofiber layers subjected to transverse pressure. The material is modeled as a structure composed of successive ideally quasi-2D nanofiber layers, with minimal out-of-plane interpenetration. Each layer consists of randomly oriented fibers that interact primarily in-plane, with limited contact to adjacent layers.

While the model employs integer transitions (i-steps) during compression due to the presence of ideal finite boxes, in reality, interpenetration and new contact generation occur from the moment of stress application on the material. Considering that the electrical resistance of the material is inversely proportional to the total number of contacts and the pressure is inversely proportional to the thickness, we can obtain the trend reported in Fig. S5, which can be fitted with a power law with exponent -1.022 (R 2  = 0.9994). The consistency between the experimental data reported in Fig.  4  and the model indicates the central role that, in a percolation regime, the formation of new contacts between nanofibers plays in improving electrical conductivity under compressive stress.

sections.heading: Mechanical Characterization
paragraphs: Figure  5  reports the stress–strain curves of PEDOT nonwoven samples obtained from uniaxial tensile tests. The specimens can be considered macroscopically homogeneous and isotropic based on the uniform distribution of randomly oriented fibers at the micro level (Fig.  S1 d). From the stress–strain curves, we can derive material parameters, such as the strength, strain at failure, and the Young’s modulus, which result in (0.30 ± 0.01) MPa, (2.1% ± 0.4%), and (16 ± 5) MPa, respectively, for as-spun samples, and (6.9 ± 1.8) MPa, (2.6% ± 0.7%), and (294 ± 145) MPa, respectively, for nonwovens after thermal treatment, as reported in Table  1 . From these data, thermal treatment emerges as an effective process to improve the mechanical properties, especially the load-bearing capability and stiffness, which increase by about 20 times without compromising the deformation capability. In recent studies, annealing of nanofiber mats at elevated temperatures has been reported as an effective strategy to improve several of their properties, including the mechanical ones, as it promotes compactness, inter-fiber fusion, and chain cross-linking, which have beneficial effects on strength and stiffness [ 44 ,  45 ]. Fig. 5 Mechanical characterization.  a  Schematic of the tensile testing platform used to derive the  b  stress–strain curves of as-spun and thermally treated PEDOT samples. Optical images of an as-spun  c , d  and thermally treated  e , f  PEDOT film before and after the tensile test, respectively Table 1 Material properties of the PEDOT-based nonwovens obtained from the uniaxial tensile test Property As-spun PEDOT Thermally treated PEDOT Maximum Stress (kPa) 303 ± 14 6865 ± 1776 Maximum Strain (%) 2.1 ± 0.4 2.6 ± 0.7 Young's Modulus (MPa) 16 ± 5 294 ± 145

The values we found for the strength and Young’s modulus are in the range of data reported in the literature for other electrospun materials. For example, PEDOT nanofiber mats prepared via electrospinning combined with in situ polymerization resulted in a tensile strength of (8.7 ± 0.4) MPa and a Young's modulus of (28.4 ± 3.3) MPa [ 46 ]. Furthermore, mats obtained from electrospinning of poly (propylene carbonate) (PPC) composites showed a tensile strength of 2 − 12 MPa and a Young’s modulus of 55 − 747 MPa, depending on the annealing methods [ 47 ]. Regarding the deformation capability, we found that the electrospun mats fail at strains less than 3%. Indeed, PEDOT, as well as its popular complex with poly(styrene sulfonate) (PEDOT:PSS), has been typically reported with limited deformation capability in its native form, motivating a spread of research aimed at enhancing its stretchability, such as via blending with other polymers and tuning their optimal concentrations [ 19 ,  48 ].

sections.heading: Ecotoxicity
paragraphs: The environmental compatibility of PEDOT nonwoven was investigated through an ecotoxicological approach. Ecotoxicology is a valuable tool for environmental monitoring and for assessing the effects of different stressors (including nanomaterials and nanofibers, e.g., Refs. [ 49 ,  50 – 51 ]) by applying standardized, sensitive, quick, and reliable bioassays [ 52 ].

Despite the reduced mobility of nanomaterials incorporated into a solid matrix, nanofibers can be released into the environment under specific conditions, such as mechanical stress, weathering, washing, and direct contact, thereby posing a potential ecological risk [ 53 ]. Considering the solubility and environmental stability of PEDOT [ 54 ], we developed, for the first time, a leaching protocol to assess the potential toxicity of nonwoven materials towards aquatic ecosystems. To this end, marine and freshwater species, representative of the first trophic levels, were exposed to PEDOT leachates. The ecotoxicological results are reported in Fig.  6 . Specifically, bacteria exhibited an effect, in terms of bioluminescence inhibition, after 30 min of exposure to leachates (resulting in 23.8% and 14.9% inhibition in as-spun and thermally treated PEDOT, respectively; see Table  2 ), which was not significantly different from the controls ( p  > 0.05). No toxicity was observed in freshwater and marine crustacean and algal species, as effects < 10% were observed after 48 h or 72 h exposure to both untreated and thermally treated PEDOT, and these effects were not significantly different from the controls ( p  > 0.05). Fig. 6 Percentage and relative standard error of leachate effect of as-spun PEDOT (light grey bars) and thermally treated PEDOT (dark grey bars) nonwovens towards aquatic (marine, freshwater) bacteria ( Aliivibrio fischeri),  microalgae  (Phaeodactylum tricornutum, Raphidocelis subcapitata ), and crustaceans ( Artemia franciscana, Daphnia magna ) after the exposure to leachates and controls (white bars). Our findings demonstrate the lack of toxicity of both as-spun and thermally treated PEDOT in freshwater and marine ecosystems, since the ecotoxicological responses obtained in bacteria, phyto- and zooplankton did not significantly differ from those measured in control samples (freshwater or seawater without nanofibers). These results on freshwater bacteria and phytoplankton confirm the literature data, reporting the biocompatibility of PEDOT:PSS-PEO nanofibers after 72 h of exposure [ 21 ]. Specifically, these authors did not find any toxicity in the green algae C hlamydomonas reinhardtii  up to 72 h, in line with the present study, which used another green algae species ( R. subcapitata ). Regarding bacteria, Ref. [ 21 ] reported a slight decrease in the photosynthetic parameters of the cyanobacterium  Synechocystis  sp. after 72 h. This decrease was not attributable to a toxic effect of the fibers. However, we used the bacterium  A. fischeri , and observed similar results in terms of bioluminescence inhibition after 30 min of exposure. In addition, we reported no toxicity at a high trophic level (e.g., crustaceans), which supports the eco-compatibility of as-spun and thermally treated PEDOT in the freshwater ecosystem. Accordingly, we demonstrated this issue for the first time even in the marine ecosystem, providing the absence of toxicity in the first levels of the trophic chains, including decomposers, primary producers, and secondary consumers (e.g., bacteria, microalgae, crustaceans), that serve as essential links within pelagic food webs [ 55 ]. Nonwoven materials lack acute toxicity to aquatic organisms over 72 h; however, further experiments to evaluate chronic toxicity are needed to assess the potential environmental compatibility of nonwoven materials in the aquatic ecosystems over time. In addition, the leaching method used in the present study to determine the eco compatibility of nonwoven materials was selected based on the exposure time (24 h) commonly applied to antifouling coatings [ 77 ], since no standardized protocols are available for nonwoven materials. This exposure time is also representative of material leaching lasting up to one week [ 56 ]. Still, it may not fully represent more extended leaching periods occurring in the field, where nonwoven fabrics undergo longer-term weathering driven by environmental parameters (i.e., photooxidation, salinity, mechanical, and biological degradation). The latter may change the toxicity in aquatic organisms over time; in this context, it is of great importance to assess nonwoven toxicity in the aquatic environment through long-term exposure experiments, using longer leaching times and incorporating environmental parameters. Overall, our findings contribute to increasing knowledge about the absence of PEDOT-PEO toxicity on marine and freshwater organisms, emphasizing the need for responsible development and sustainable application of emerging materials in an era of rapid technological advancement.

sections.heading: Wearable Pressure Monitoring Glove
paragraphs: The electrospun PEDOT-based material described in this contribution represents a promising innovation in the field of wearable and touch sensors. Thanks to its eco-compatibility and versatility, this material is ideal for developing wearable devices intended for use in medical and rehabilitative contexts.

This wearable prototype could assist in several clinical scenarios by targeting people with Multiple Sclerosis (PwMS). In this condition, sensory feedback and mobility are crucial, as well as post-stroke survivors with hand spasticity, patients recovering from peripheral nerve injuries, or those undergoing post-operative orthopaedic therapy. Such devices could be used alongside physical therapy practices like stretching and repetitive exercises to record real-time grip force and monitor dexterity during standard clinical assessments (e.g., hand strength, finger movements). They could also provide feedback to users during rehabilitation routines, such as grasping objects of different weights, pinching, and manipulating objects. Its ability to incorporate multipoint sensors enables precise and reliable pressure measurements, making it particularly valuable for advanced robotics and remote telemedicine. For example, sensors derived from this material can allow real-time monitoring of patient progress, providing detailed data on exerted forces and motion patterns during recovery, and resulting in personalized therapies even in the context of tele-rehabilitation. This technology can be used to create sensorized gloves that support targeted exercises and adapt to the individual needs of patients. In the robotics sector, the thermally treated PEDOT electrospun material developed in this work presents new opportunities for developing haptic devices that can simulate precise tactile sensations. These devices can be used in robotic surgical environments or operations requiring remote tactile interaction. Similarly, in telemedicine, these sensors can enhance the quality of remote diagnoses by ensuring accurate transmission of biomechanical data. The integration of this material into wearable devices not only contributes to technological advancement but also promotes the sustainable use of innovative materials. To illustrate this, we constructed several wearable pressure sensors, and used them to develop a prototype sensorised glove for demonstration purposes.

sections.heading: Pressure Sensor Evaluation
paragraphs: Based on the concept described in Sect.  4.7 , the sensor was built by placing the PEDOT-based nonwoven material between two copper electrodes and sealing it with Kapton tape, as shown schematically in Fig.  7 a. The assembled sensor (Fig.  7 b) is characterized by measuring the electrical resistance between the two copper contacts as a function of the applied load, especially in the context of cyclic stability (Fig.  7 c). Figure  7 d-f show the stability of change in electrical resistance when 10, 20, or 50 g are placed on top of the sensor. In comparison Fig.  7 g presents the consistency of change with sequential increasing loads. Fig. 7 a  Pressure sensor scheme and  b  Prototype.  c  Cyclic stability under compressive load. By applying different calibrated weights to the sensor, the characterization curves  d ,  e , and  f  are obtained from repeated measurements.  g  Comparison of the relative resistance of the generated signal with sequentially increasing weights

It is worth noting that, as expected, the reported trend in relative electric resistance with increasing applied weights is consistent with the electrochemical characterization of nonwovens reported in Fig.  4 e.

Compared with previously reported PEDOT:PSS-based pressure sensors (see Table  3 ), the nonwoven PEDOT:PSS–PEO material developed in this work demonstrates a balanced and competitive performance across sensitivity, operating range, and durability. In resistance mode, our sensor exhibits a sensitivity of –0.024 kPa −1 , which exceeds the magnitude reported for both the PEDOT:PSS–PI conductive aerogel (0.019 kPa −1 ) and the EtOH-optimized PEDOT:PSS nanocoating on microstructured PDMS (–0.016 kPa −1 ). The aerogel system of Zhao et al. benefits from high compressibility but suffers from limited cycle stability (200 cycles), whereas our nonwoven structure achieves a fivefold improvement (1,000 cycles) while also supporting a slightly wider pressure range (20 kPa vs. 18 kPa) [ 58 ]. Compared with Lee et al. [ 62 ], whose ultrathin PEDOT:PSS coating is optimized for ultralow-pressure detection (≤ 1 kPa) with excellent cycling stability, our sensor provides a sensitivity approximately 50% higher while operating over a substantially broader pressure window (20 × larger). Notably, achieving such sensitivity without reliance on microstructured substrates or fragile aerogel architectures highlights the advantage of the nonwoven PEDOT:PSS–PEO network, which offers conformal fiber-level deformation, stable conductive pathways, and robust mechanical compliance. Overall, the performance comparison underscores that this work delivers an effective compromise between high sensitivity, practical pressure range, and mechanical robustness.

sections.heading: Wearable Demonstrator Testing
paragraphs: Glove assembly (Fig.  8 a-c) has been conducted by connecting the prototype PCB board, hosting the ESP32-S3 MCU, battery, and the resistors to each ADC channel, as schematically shown in Fig.  8 d. Each sensor has been tested using multiple finger taps, monitored via a USB serial monitor in the Arduino Software IDE, as shown in Fig.  8 e, which reports the response curve for the sensor located on the thumb. When the voltage level, measured continuously for each sensor, surpasses its minimum threshold, a blue indicator appears on the display for the corresponding finger (Fig.  8 f-h). When it exceeds its maximum threshold, the same indicator turns red on display, as shown in Fig.  8 i. This enables quick visual feedback on whether each finger is applying pressure within the target range. Fig. 8 a , b , c  Assembly of the sensorized glove.  d  Schematic diagram of prototype board connection on the demonstrator glove and  e  Acquired signal. Detail of the onboard LCD screen without any pressure  f , g , and with blue  h  and red  i  markers on the fingers, indicating the correct pressure level and the overload, respectively. An example of blue and red thresholds is shown on the acquired signal

When evaluating the sensorized glove demonstrator, it is essential to consider the primary biomechanical hand grip positions widely discussed in the scientific literature [ 63 ,  64 ,  65 – 66 ]. In manual grasp studies, identifying and classifying primary grip types used in daily life and industrial applications is crucial. Among these, two of the most relevant grips are the precision and power grip. The precision grip, typically involved in manipulating small objects such as tweezers or needles, predominantly engages the thumb and index finger, enabling fine movement control. This grip is of great importance in rehabilitative medicine for restoring dexterity in patients affected by neurological or musculoskeletal injuries, where the relevance of force and coordination analysis is crucial in hand rehabilitation protocols. Conversely, the power grip is essential for activities that require substantial force, such as grasping a glass or lifting a dumbbell. In the field of prosthetics and anthropomorphic robotics, the faithful reproduction of the power grip remains a significant challenge, as it is crucial for allowing users of advanced prostheses to perform everyday tasks safely and naturally [ 67 ,  68 ].

The practical application of these insights is evident in the development of wearable devices, such as the sensorized glove developed here, which is capable of real-time monitoring of grip quality and force during rehabilitation exercises or providing haptic feedback in new-generation myoelectric prosthetic hands. For instance, state-of-the-art prosthetic control systems integrate pressure sensors to relay tactile information to the user, thereby enhancing dexterity and safety during manipulation. In robotics, replicating human biomechanical grip strategies has enabled the design of robotic hands capable of performing complex movements, such as the gentle manipulation of fragile objects. This is achieved by integrating advanced sensors and control algorithms inspired by human physiology. Figure S6 illustrates the glove behavior with fingertip color feedback while executing routine actions such as tapping (Fig. S6a-c and video in SI), as well as key biomechanical grips, including precision pinch (Fig. S6d) and grasping a glass (Fig. S6e-f), thereby simulating typical movements encountered in rehabilitation procedures or robotic manipulation tasks. These actions demonstrate the adaptability of the glove in providing color-based feedback during various functional hand movements.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study developed eco-friendly, free-standing conductive nonwovens based on PEDOT:PSS and PEO for flexible and wearable electronics. Thermal treatment was shown to markedly improve their conductivity and mechanical performance while preserving environmental compatibility. Comprehensive electrical, mechanical, and ecotoxicological evaluations confirmed their suitability for advanced applications, with no significant toxicity observed in freshwater or marine organisms. The materials’ practical potential was demonstrated through a rehabilitation glove equipped with PEDOT-based pressure sensors, which delivered reliable and precise measurements. These results underscore the promise of sustainable conductive polymers for next-generation wearable devices. Limitations of the current work include the need for improved long-term stability under real-world conditions and broader testing across diverse sensing scenarios, beside addressing the challenges in large-scale production of conductive nonwovens. Future research should focus on optimizing sensor performance, addressing real-world conditions robustness, integrating additional functionalities, and expanding environmental impact assessments to support safe, scalable adoption of these materials.

sections.heading: Material Synthesis and Characterization
paragraphs:
Two commercially available water dispersions of PEDOT (namely PH1000 and T2) have been selected for the optimization of the electrospinning parameters. The two dispersions have different electrical conductivity, with PH1000 reaching up to 850 S·cm −1  while T2 presenting conductivities in the order of a few S·cm −1  [ 69 ]. PEDOT:PSS PH1000 or T2 1.3% wt water dispersions, produced by Heraeus, have been mixed with PEO 600 kDa from Sigma Aldrich and deionized water to prepare PEDOT-based water solutions with different PEDOT/PSS/PEO ratios (see Table  4 ). Various amounts of PEO and PEDOT:PSS were stirred overnight at 2500 r·min −1  in water for the preparation of the solutions, and subsequently, poured into a 20 mL glass syringe for the electrospinning process.
 Table 4 Composition of PEDOT-based solutions ID Raw Material PEDOT Concentration [mol·l −1 ] PSS Concentration [mol·l −1 ] PEO Concentration [mol·l −1 ] PEO:PSS Ratio 1 PH1000 2.65E-03 2.32E-05 9.17E-05 3.95 2 PH1000 1.77E-03 1.55E-05 6.11E-05 3.95 3 PH1000 2.29E-03 2.00E-05 7.90E-05 3.95 4 PH1000 2.01E-03 1.76E-05 6.94E-05 3.95 5 PH1000 1.12E-03 9.82E-06 6.41E-05 6.53 6 PH1000 6.71E-04 5.87E-06 3.83E-05 6.53 7 PH1000 1.72E-03 1.50E-05 6.15E-05 4.10 8 T2 1.59E-03 1.39E-05 8.89E-05 6.38 9 T2 2.65E-03 2.32E-05 6.67E-05 2.87 10 T2 1.33E-03 1.16E-05 5.56E-05 4.79 11 T2 2.21E-03 1.93E-05 8.33E-05 4.31 12 T2 1.82E-03 1.60E-05 8.33E-05 5.22 13 T2 2.06E-03 1.81E-05 5.56E-05 3.08

Nonwoven samples were fabricated using a Linari RT Advanced electrospinning apparatus in a roll-to-roll configuration. The working distance between the syringe needle and the aluminum foil collector was set to 15 cm. The electrospinning process was carried out at a voltage of 17 kV and a flow rate of 0.1 mL·h −1 . After 6 h of continuous electrospinning, the process was stopped, and the resulting sample was left to dry overnight inside the electrospinning chamber (temperature of 25 °C and RH = 20%) before characterization. Copper gaskets (61.1 mm outer diameter) have been used as supportive rings during the electrospinning of free-standing samples (see Fig.  9 ). Free-standing PEDOT-based nonwovens eliminate the mechanical constraints and interfacial failures associated with solid substrates, allowing the entire porous 3D network to deform uniformly under pressure for enhanced electromechanical sensitivity; these features give PEDOT-based free-standing nonwovens a compelling advantage as lightweight, conformable, and mechanically robust platforms for pressure and strain sensing, especially in applications where substrate-supported systems may suffer from restricted deformation, poor adhesion, or reduced long-term durability [ 70 ,  71 – 72 ]. Their substrate-free architecture also improves flexibility, conformability, and long-term durability while simplifying fabrication and enabling lightweight, breathable, and easily integrable sensing platforms. After spinning, a portion of the free-standing samples has been thermally treated in vacuum (2 mbar) with a first stage at 70 °C for one hour and then a second stage at 125 °C for two hours. Temperature ramps between stages were 5 °C·min −1 . The first step at 70 °C (near the melting point of PEO) enhances chain mobility and allows limited structural relaxation while maintaining the integrity of the nanofiber morphology. The second step at 125 °C lies within the temperature range where condensation or etherification between PEO hydroxyl groups and PSS sulfonic acid groups has been reported [ 73 ,  74 ]. At this stage, sulfonate-ester (S–O–C) bonds can form, providing interpolymer crosslinking without compromising the nanofiber structure. Fig. 9 a  Free-standing sample fabrication setup scheme using copper ring targets.  b  Electron microscope image of the free-standing nanofibers, using secondary electron mode, working distance of 8 mm, electron high tension of 20 kV, and magnification of 10. 5 x.  c  Overlay of the EDX concentration map for sulfur element (in red)

Viscosity : Rheological measurements were conducted using a DSR 500 CP-4000 Plus rheometer (Lamy Rheology, France). The viscosity of the starting solutions was assessed by subjecting them to increasing and decreasing shear-rate ramps ranging from 10 to 500 s⁻ 1 .

Differential Scanning Calorimetry : Thermograms of raw materials and electrospun nonwovens have been performed using a DSC 250 (TA Instruments). Samples (1.5–2 mg each) have been placed in Al pans and heated, cooled, and reheated from −40 °C to 150 °C at a rate of 10 °C·min −1 .
Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy : Spectra have been collected with a Bruker Vertex 70 from 4000 to 500 cm −1 , 128 scans with a resolution of 2 cm −1 .

X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy : XPS spectra were recorded using a PHI ESCA 5600 MultiTechnique apparatus equipped with a monochromatic Al kα source (1486.6 eV) with an analysis spot of approximately 150 µm. The X-ray source and analyzer are at 90°, and the sample surface is set at 45°. Survey scans were acquired with a pass energy of 137 eV to maximize sensitivity, while high-resolution narrow regions were recorded at 23.5 eV. The spectra have been analyzed using CasaXPS software. PEDOT S 2p doublet has been fitted using LA(1,2.85,60) lineshape, all other peaks using LA(50). Backgrounds are evaluated with a Shirley algorithm.

Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM): SEM  was used to image the nonwoven samples after electro-spinning. Both a Zeiss EVO 40 (Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany) equipped with Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS, Cambridge INCA 300 with PentaFET EDXS detector sensitive to light elements, Z > 5; Oxford Instruments, Oxfordshire, U.K.) and a Hitachi TM4000 Plus (Tokyo, Japan) at an accelerating voltage of 10–15 kV have been used. The thickness of the fabricated nonwovens was evaluated from cross-sectional images taken with a JEOL IT300 SEM. Before SEM inspection, the sample was cooled in liquid nitrogen, carefully broken with tweezers, and then attached to a standard SEM sample holder using double-sided conductive tape.

Cyclic Voltammetry and Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) : Electrochemical measurements were performed using a Solartron 1287 potentiostat/galvanostat coupled with a Solartron 1260 frequency response analyzer (Solartron Analytical, Farnborough, UK). Tests were carried out on samples mounted on an ItalSense IS-C screen-printed carbon electrode (SPE, purchased from PalmSens B.V., Netherlands) and immersed in a naturally aerated 0.1 mol·l −1  sodium chloride solution (VWR, AnalaR NORMAPUR, purity > 99.5%) at room temperature. The SPE included the sample as the working electrode (WE), an Ag reference electrode (RE), and a carbon counter electrode (CE). The electrochemical characterization consisted of the performance of cyclic voltammetries in the potential range −1 to 1 V vs Ag with the scan rates 10, 20, and 50 mV·s −1 . Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy was measured before and after the CV characterization, at the open-circuit potential, in the frequency range of 200 kHz – 0.1 Hz in potentiostatic mode, with an AC signal of 10 mV applied.

Electromechanical response : A custom experimental setup was used to characterize the electro-mechanical response of the investigated materials (see Fig. S7). The device consisted of an integrated electro-mechanical testing system, enabling the simultaneous application of a controlled mechanical pressure while making electrical measurements. The mechanical loading was provided by compressed air, applying controlled pressure to the sample positioned between two stainless steel plungers coated with gold to enhance electrical contact. Electrical measurements were performed using a four-wire sensing connection circuit through four leads connected to a Solartron 1260 frequency response analyzer for AC impedance measurements. This configuration eliminated resistance contributions from the wires, ensuring accurate electrical characterization. Electrical measurements were carried out at an open-circuit voltage in the frequency range of 500 kHz to 1 Hz, in potentiostatic mode, with an AC signal amplitude of 10 mV. Samples were characterized with and without pressure, applying loads between 50 and 200 g·cm −2 .

Tensile tests : The PEDOT-based free-standing nonwovens that were prepared were characterized from a mechanical point of view using a custom-made uniaxial tensile testing platform [ 75 ]. The setup consists of a linear range (actuator) and a load sensor (calibrated spring) with attached silicon pieces supporting the specimen. The setup was mounted under an optical microscope to capture the displacement of silicon pieces, and the displacement values were obtained by analyzing the captured images using a custom-made image correlation software written in C. Rectangular specimens with dimensions of approximately (3 ± 0.5) mm (gauge length) and approximately (2 ± 0.5) mm (width) were cut using a razor blade from the same batch of prepared samples. The thickness of the as-spun PEDOT and thermally treated PEDOT nonwovens was measured using SEM analysis, resulting in values of (29 ± 2) µm and (5 ± 2) µm, respectively. The cross-sectional area was obtained by multiplying the thickness and width of the specimen at the initial or undeformed configuration. The specimen was glued to the silicon pieces (which act as the grips), and subsequently, displacement was applied through the linear range. The nominal strain is computed as the ratio of the relative displacement of the silicon pieces and the gauge length of the specimen. The force acting on the specimen is calculated from the displacement of the spring multiplied by its calibrated spring constant. Consequently, nominal stress was obtained as the ratio of the force and the cross-sectional area. Young’s modulus of the samples was calculated as the slope of the stress–strain curve in its initial region [ 76 ]. A minimum of five specimens that failed near the mid-gauge section of the specimen were considered to obtain the average and standard deviation of calibrated material parameters. All specimens were characterized at room temperature (approximately 20 °C).

sections.heading: Ecotoxicity Screening
paragraphs: The environmental compatibility of as-spun and thermally treated PEDOT nonwovens was evaluated in freshwater and seawater through ecotoxicological tests. Indeed, the latter can be used to measure material leachate toxicity as a tool for indirect field efficacy evaluation [ 77 ,  78 ]. Since no standard leaching protocols have been developed explicitly for nanostructured nonwovens, leaching products were obtained by following the ASTM D6442 and the protocol proposed by Gadkari et al., with minor modifications to maximize the sample surface-to-water volume ratio during leaching [ 79 ,  80 ]. Briefly, as-spun and thermally treated PEDOT samples of 2 cm × 2 cm were suspended in 30 mL filtered natural sea water (FNSW, 0.22 µm) or standard freshwater (ISO 6341) for marine and freshwater bioassays, respectively [ 81 ]. The suspensions were then placed on an orbital shaker at 120 r·min −1  to mimic field turbulence and incubated in the dark at 20 °C for 24 h. After this period, the leachates were filtered using a vacuum filtration system equipped with microfiber filters (Whatman GF/F filters 0.45 μm). The resulting solutions were directly used for the ecotoxicological bioassays.

sections.heading: Bacteria
paragraphs: The bioluminescence inhibition of the photobacterium  Aliivibrio fischeri  was assessed according to the UNI EN ISO 11348–3 protocol [ 82 ]. The lyophilized bacteria were kept at −20 °C before testing and activated by hydration. Bioassays were carried out in triplicates by exposing bacteria to leachates. All the samples were kept on a thermostatic plate at 15 °C throughout the entire test. The negative control was performed by NaCl solution. Leachates toxicity was measured after 30-min incubation by Microtox™ 500 luminometer. Data were then analysed using MicrotoxOmni software. Samples were considered toxic when a 50% reduction in the light output (vs. control) was obtained.

sections.heading: Phytoplankton
paragraphs: The growth inhibition tests of the marine diatom  Phaeodactylum tricornutum , and the freshwater green  alga Raphidocelis subcapitata  were carried out according to standardized protocols (ISO 10253/2016), OECD 201 (2011), UNI EN ISO-8692:2012), modified by using multi-well plates [ 83 ,  84 ,  85 – 86 ]. Specifically,  P. tricornutum  was obtained from the CNR-IAS laboratories culture collection, while  R. subcapitata  stock culture was purchased from MicroBioTests Inc. (Gent, Belgium). Bioassays were performed by exposing the algae to leachates of as-spun and thermally treated PEDOT for 72 h at (20 ± 0.5) °C with a 12:12 light:dark photoperiod and light intensity of 6000–10000 lx. Three replicates were performed for leachates and negative control (algal growth medium). Algal growth was blocked by adding Lugol’s solution after 72 h. The cells were then counted under an inverted microscope (Leitz Diavert, Germany) by using a haemocytometer (Bürker chamber). Finally, the growth inhibition percentage was calculated by comparing the algal growth in the test solutions with that of the negative control.

sections.heading: Zooplankton
paragraphs: Immobility was evaluated in marine and freshwater crustaceans. Regarding marine crustaceans, certified dehydrated cysts of  Artemia franciscana  were purchased from MicroBioTests Inc. (Belgium) and used for the experiments. Briefly, 500 mg of cyst suspension was incubated for 48 h at 28 °C under a light source (3000 ÷ 4000 lx) in FNSW (37 ‰ salinity) to obtain larvae. The larvae were then separated from non-hatched cysts and transferred into a beaker with FNSW to a final concentration of 15–20 organisms·mL −1 . The bioassays were carried out by adding 15–20 nauplii into each well of 24 multi-well plates containing 1 mL of leachates of as-spun and thermally treated PEDOT nonwovens by using a small 80 µm mesh filter. Four replicates, including the control, were performed. The plates were then incubated in the dark for 48 h at 25 °C. After this exposure time, immobility was checked under a stereomicroscope.

Regarding freshwater crustaceans,  Daphnia magna  was purchased from MicroBioTests Inc. (Belgium) through the Daphtoxkit F TM magna (1996). The bioassays were carried out by following Standard Operational Procedures in multi-well plates. Specifically, 9 mL of test solution and 5 daphnid neonates for each well were used. Four replicates, including the control, were performed. The plates were then incubated for 48 h at (20 ± 0.5) °C in darkness to evaluate immobility, as described above for marine crustaceans.

sections.heading: Statistical data analysis
paragraphs: All ecotoxicological data are expressed as mean ± standard error (SE) of the triplicates. The nonparametric Wilcoxon test was applied to determine any significant differences between controls and treated samples. Data was considered significantly different when  p  < 0.05. All analyses were performed using R statistical software (R version 4.0.2).

sections.heading: Pressure Sensor Manufacturing and Wearable Demonstrator Development
paragraphs: Each pressure sensor intended for use in the sensorized glove was made by cutting a 5 mm × 5 mm square of freestanding electrospun PEDOT nonwoven and placing it between two thin, flexible copper electrodes. Two outer layers of adhesive Kapton tape were used to hold the contacts in place and seal the sensor assembly. All the materials used in the glove assembly (cotton, Kapton tape) are generally considered skin-safe [ 87 ,  88 ]. Sensor characterization was performed by measuring the electrical resistance between the two copper contacts as a function of the applied load (Fig.  10 ). Fig. 10 Concept of the nonwoven material as force sensing resistor

The demonstrator was constructed by attaching five pressure sensors, one for each fingertip, that embed the electrospun PEDOT-based nonwoven as a functional layer within a dermatologic cotton glove. Kapton-covered copper wires 0.125 mm in diameter were embroidered through the internal side of the glove and electrically connected, on one side, to the pressure sensors via Molex connectors, for easy replacement, and, on the other side, to the control electronic board. A Waveshare ESP32-S3-LCD-1.3 development board was chosen for its cost-effectiveness and high performance; it features a 12-bit ADC and micro-SD card control for acquiring and storing sensor data. Power supply was guaranteed by a PL4054 lithium battery manager. The acquisition and control software has been developed using the Arduino Software IDE Version 2.3.6 (the source code is available from the authors on reasonable request). All measurements were conducted under controlled laboratory conditions, and the sensor’s encapsulated configuration minimizes environmental fluctuations, ensuring that temperature- and humidity-related effects remain negligible within the scope of this study.
